data: Sputnik 1 (1957). Vostok 1 — Gagarin (1961). Five hundred and forty Soyuz launches from a single pad.

Soviet R-7 era pad at Baikonur Cosmodrome. Sputnik 1 (October 4, 1957), Vostok 1 (Gagarin, April 12, 1961), every Vostok crewed flight, every Voskhod, and the bulk of the Soyuz manifest through to the final crew launch on September 25, 2019 (Soyuz MS-15). Preserved as a museum monument; the 2019-era refurbishment plan was abandoned when the site was transferred to Kazakhstan in 2025. Coordinates from Roscosmos and US Naval Observatory records.

The single most historically significant orbital launch pad in the world. R-7 ICBM test stand from 1957; immediately repurposed for Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957 — the start of the Space Age. Yuri Gagarin lifted from here on April 12, 1961. Every Vostok crew, every Voskhod, the bulk of all Soyuz manifests through to MS-15 in September 2019. Five hundred and forty launches from one pad over sixty-two years. Preserved as a museum monument; the 2019-era refurbishment plan was abandoned when the site was transferred to Kazakhstan in 2025.
First artificial satellite to orbit Earth — start of the Space Age
First human in space; first crewed orbital flight
First day in space — 17 orbits over 25 hours
First dual-flight rendezvous — flew within ~6.5 km of Vostok 4
Second half of first dual flight — first communications between two crewed spacecraft
Longest solo Earth-orbital flight — 4 days 23 hours, 81 orbits
First woman in space — Valentina Tereshkova, 48 orbits
First multi-crew spaceflight — three cosmonauts in a Vostok-derived capsule
First crewed Soyuz flight — parachute failure killed Vladimir Komarov (first in-flight spaceflight death)
First crew to a space station (Salyut 1); all 3 died of decompression on reentry
Carried Sputnik and Gagarin to orbit
Soviet R-7-derived launcher that put Gagarin in space — Vostok 1 (1961-04-12) and 5 more Vostok flights through 1963
Vostok-K successor — more thrust for the heavier Voskhod capsule. Launched Voskhod 1 (1964) + Voskhod 2 (1965 Leonov EVA)
R-7-derived launcher for the first-generation Soyuz spacecraft — flew Soyuz 1 (1967) and Soyuz 11 (1971)
First Soyuz generation; Komarov's fatal flight
Active Soyuz crewed pad — every ISS Soyuz crew rotation since 2020 has lifted from Site 31
Baikonur's Proton complex: Proton 1, Salyut 1, Mir and ISS modules, Mars and Luna probes
Russia's northern military cosmodrome — more launches than any other site
Plesetsk's workhorse Soyuz pad at 62.9°N — the world's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex
Proton pad — the Mir core, Salyut 7, Nauka, and probes from Venera to ExoMars
Russia's Soyuz-2 pad in the Far East: first launch 2016, OneWeb batches, Luna 25 (2023)
